title: Zuriel Chapter Introductions — Leviticus 11–27
description: Seventeen chapter-specific study guides covering ritual status, restoration, atonement, holiness, justice, appointed feasts, land rest, covenant blessings and vows.

chapters.title: Leviticus 11 — Clean and unclean animals
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 11 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on food distinctions, land animals, water creatures, birds and swarming creatures. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter classifies creatures by stated criteria, regulates contact with carcasses, and concludes with Israel's call to holiness.
chapters.studyObservation: Follow each category separately and note how the text distinguishes ordinary food choices from temporary ritual status after contact with carcasses.
chapters.connectionNotes: Deuteronomy 14 restates Israel's food distinctions; Mark 7 and Acts 10 address defilement and Gentile inclusion in later settings that must be read on their own terms.
studyQuestions: What criteria distinguish the land animals and water creatures?
What happens after contact with an unclean carcass?
How does the chapter explain Israel's call to holiness?
chapters.lifeApplication: Let daily habits express thoughtful belonging without using food choices to rank another person's spiritual worth or shame those with different practices.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Ritual cleanness is not moral worth, and this is not a modern nutrition guide. Christian interpretations differ; preserve the original Israelite covenant setting.
chapters.readingNote: Read the categories and the rationale in verses 44–47, then compare Deuteronomy 14 and Peter's explanation in Acts 10 without flattening their different contexts.

chapters.title: Leviticus 12 — Purification after childbirth
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 12 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on childbirth, blood, sanctuary access and prescribed offerings within ancient Israel's ritual system. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter sets out periods of ritual status after childbirth and an offering brought at the tent of meeting, with a less costly bird offering for a household unable to afford a lamb.
chapters.studyObservation: The text gives a defined process and an explicit provision for differing means. Ritual uncleanness is temporary status, not an accusation that childbirth is sinful or shameful.
chapters.connectionNotes: Luke 2:22–24 refers to the offering after Jesus' birth; read it as a narrative of observance within Israel rather than a claim that childbirth itself is sinful.
studyQuestions: How do the stated periods differ after the birth of a son and daughter?
What offering and less costly alternative are provided?
Why must ritual status not be confused with moral guilt?
chapters.lifeApplication: Treat mothers and families with dignity, practical care and compassion during recovery, and notice how the law makes provision for limited resources.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not interpret postpartum ritual status as guilt, rejection or a medical diagnosis. The ancient ritual rule does not authorise discrimination or neglect of women.
chapters.readingNote: Compare the prescribed periods and offerings with Luke 2:22–24, keeping ritual status distinct from moral blame and attending to the provision for a poorer household.

chapters.title: Leviticus 13 — Skin conditions and affected garments
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 13 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on visible skin conditions, garments, priestly inspection and the community's ritual boundaries. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter gives procedures for examining swelling, eruptions, burns, chronic conditions and affected garments; cases may require isolation, washing, reassessment or removal.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the repeated pattern of inspection, waiting and reassessment. Priests classify ritual status; the chapter is not offering modern clinical diagnoses.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 14 describes restoration after healing. Gospel accounts of Jesus healing people with skin conditions highlight healing and restored community participation in a different setting.
studyQuestions: What observations lead to isolation and later reassessment?
How are garments examined differently from skin?
What cautions guide modern interpretation of these ancient categories?
chapters.lifeApplication: Respond to illness and visible difference with patience, dignity and practical support; avoid quick judgements about another person's condition or spiritual life.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The Hebrew ritual category often translated leprosy does not always mean Hansen's disease. This is not a diagnostic manual and must not be used to stigmatise people.
chapters.readingNote: Compare the inspection periods with Leviticus 14 and note that the rules concern garments as well as people, so the chapter covers several kinds of suspected condition.

chapters.title: Leviticus 14 — Cleansing and restoration
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 14 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on the restoration of people declared clean after skin conditions and the examination of affected houses. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter describes a staged restoration ceremony with birds, washing and offerings, provides for a person of limited means, and gives procedures for examining and treating affected houses.
chapters.studyObservation: Restoration is a process, not merely a label. The house procedure includes inspection and removal of affected materials, with demolition only when the condition persists.
chapters.connectionNotes: Chapter 13 supplies the preceding examination rules. Gospel healing accounts and Hebrews 9 use cleansing imagery in distinct narrative and theological contexts.
studyQuestions: What stages mark a person's restoration?
How does the law provide for limited financial means?
What steps are taken when a house is affected?
chapters.lifeApplication: Make room for people to return to community after illness or hardship; restoration should include practical support, patience and dignity.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not invent hidden meanings for every ritual item. House procedures are not modern building standards, and ancient disease terms should not be mapped carelessly onto present diagnoses.
chapters.readingNote: Read the person's restoration ceremony alongside the house instructions, including the reduced offering, and keep the chapter connected to the inspection process in chapter 13.

chapters.title: Leviticus 15 — Bodily discharges and ritual status
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 15 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on male and female bodily discharges, contact, washing and sanctuary-centred ritual cleanness. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter describes how discharges affect persons, bedding, seats and contacts, sets washing and waiting periods, and specifies offerings when an abnormal discharge ends.
chapters.studyObservation: Distinguish ordinary bodily processes from unusual or prolonged conditions. The text does not treat every case identically and concludes by explaining the sanctuary concern.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 12 and 13 also address bodily conditions. Mark 5:25–34 portrays Jesus healing a woman with a flow of blood and restoring her dignity.
studyQuestions: Which conditions are treated separately?
What washing and waiting procedures recur?
How does ritual language differ from moral condemnation?
chapters.lifeApplication: Treat health matters with discretion, compassion and respect; do not shame people for natural processes or make care conditional on religious performance.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Ritual uncleanness is not moral wrongdoing. These ancient procedures are not medical advice and must not be used to stigmatise menstruation, illness or disability.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the categories in order and note where normal cycles are distinguished from unusual conditions; then consider the healing and restoration in Mark 5.

chapters.title: Leviticus 16 — The Day of Atonement
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 16 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on the annual sanctuary rite following the deaths of Aaron's sons and the warning about entering the inner sanctuary. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The high priest makes offerings for himself and the people, uses two goats with distinct roles, and participates in the cleansing of the sanctuary and altar; the day is marked by rest and self-denial.
chapters.studyObservation: Follow the sequence and distinguish the roles of the two goats. The rite addresses the sanctuary and the people's wrongdoing, and specifies who may enter the innermost space and when.
chapters.connectionNotes: Hebrews 9–10 interprets sanctuary and sacrifice in relation to Christ's priestly work. Read that Christian theology as a later interpretation rooted in, but not identical to, Leviticus.
studyQuestions: Why does the chapter begin with a warning about entering the inner sanctuary?
What distinct roles do the two goats have?
Which parts of the rite address the sanctuary and which address the people?
chapters.lifeApplication: Take confession, reconciliation and accountable leadership seriously, and recognise the care with which the chapter treats sacred responsibility.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not claim the chapter itself settles every later theory of atonement or reduce both goats to one simplistic metaphor; preserve its ritual structure and Israelite setting.
chapters.readingNote: Read the opening warning with the detailed sequence and compare Hebrews 9, noting both the shared imagery and the distinct theological setting.

chapters.title: Leviticus 17 — The sanctity of blood
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 17 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on sacrificial slaughter, sanctuary centrality and the prohibition on consuming blood. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter regulates where sacrificial animals are slaughtered, rejects offerings to other powers, prohibits consuming blood, and explains that blood is associated with life and given on the altar for atonement.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the relationship between blood, life and the altar in the chapter's own explanation. The rules apply to Israelites and resident foreigners and distinguish sacrificial slaughter from hunting.
chapters.connectionNotes: Genesis 9:4–6 contains earlier blood language; Deuteronomy 12 addresses slaughter in the land; Hebrews 9 reflects on blood and purification in a later Christian argument.
studyQuestions: Why does the chapter centralise sacrificial slaughter?
How does the text explain blood and life?
To whom do the blood restrictions apply?
chapters.lifeApplication: Value life and approach worship with reverence; let concern for life encourage responsible treatment of others rather than excusing harm.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not convert ancient sacrificial rules into modern dietary or medical claims or detach the statement about blood from its ritual setting.
chapters.readingNote: Compare verses 10–14 with Genesis 9 and Deuteronomy 12, observing how the rule is framed within Israel's sanctuary and covenant practice.

chapters.title: Leviticus 18 — Covenant boundaries and sexual conduct
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 18 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on Israel's distinct covenant life, prohibited relationships and the warning against adopting surrounding practices. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter names prohibited family relationships and sexual practices, forbids child sacrifice to Molech, and warns that such conduct defiles the land and must not be repeated by Israel.
chapters.studyObservation: Read the prohibitions within the opening and closing frame: Israel is not to imitate Egypt or Canaan but to live by the Lord's commands. Personal conduct is linked with household and communal wellbeing.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 20 revisits several prohibitions with penalties. New Testament discussions of sexual ethics belong to their own settings and should not be assumed to reproduce every detail of Israel's civil code.
studyQuestions: How does the opening frame the laws that follow?
What kinds of family and community harm are addressed?
How does the chapter connect conduct with covenant life and the land?
chapters.lifeApplication: Protect family members and vulnerable people through integrity, consent, faithfulness and responsible boundaries; recognise the harm caused by exploitation and betrayal.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Never use this chapter to justify abuse, coercion or humiliation, or to blame victims. Distinguish the ancient covenant law from modern civil law and protect vulnerable people.
chapters.readingNote: Begin with verses 1–5, examine the prohibitions and finish with the warning about the land; compare chapter 20 without assuming both chapters serve identical purposes.

chapters.title: Leviticus 19 — Holiness in everyday community life
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 19 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on worship, neighbour care, honest trade, fair judgement, gleaning and protection for the vulnerable. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter gathers commands about parents, Sabbath, offerings, gleaning, truthful dealing, justice, wages, respect for elders, care for foreigners and love of neighbour.
chapters.studyObservation: The movement between worship and daily ethics is important. Neighbour-love appears alongside fair wages, courts, harvest practices and business, so holiness shapes ordinary public and private conduct.
chapters.connectionNotes: Jesus cites neighbour-love in Matthew 22:39, and James 2 challenges favouritism. These later texts highlight ethical concerns also present in Leviticus while remaining in their own settings.
studyQuestions: Which commands connect worship with daily treatment of others?
How are poor people and resident foreigners protected?
What practical examples of neighbour-love appear?
chapters.lifeApplication: Practise fairness in business, prompt payment, truthful speech and generosity; treat neighbours and strangers with dignity and resist favouritism.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not reduce the chapter to a slogan while ignoring concrete protections for workers, poor people and foreigners; interpret individual commands in their ancient legal context.
chapters.readingNote: Read verses 9–18 as a connected pattern of neighbour care, then note the later concern for justice and honest measures; compare Jesus and James thoughtfully.

chapters.title: Leviticus 20 — Accountability and covenant consequences
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 20 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on penalties for specified offences, community responsibility and Israel's call to distinct covenant life. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter revisits prohibitions from chapter 18 and details penalties within Israel's covenant legal order, including matters involving child sacrifice, mediums and prohibited relationships.
chapters.studyObservation: Compare the repeated offences with chapter 18: the chapters are related but serve different functions. The conclusion returns to holiness and distinctions associated with Israel's covenant vocation.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 18 provides the preceding prohibitions and Deuteronomy 18 addresses related forbidden practices in another legal collection; later Christian discipline belongs to a different setting.
studyQuestions: How does chapter 20 relate to chapter 18?
What forms of communal accountability appear?
Why must ancient penalties not be treated as permission for private violence?
chapters.lifeApplication: Take accountability seriously while insisting on careful, impartial justice that protects the vulnerable; distinguish personal responsibility from collective blame.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: These penalties belong to ancient Israel's covenant legal system and never authorise private violence, vigilantism or modern religious persecution.
chapters.readingNote: Read chapter 20 alongside chapter 18, marking repeated prohibitions and added penalties, then consider the closing call to Israel's distinct covenant identity.

chapters.title: Leviticus 21 — Priestly holiness and responsibility
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 21 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on the conduct and ritual responsibilities of ordinary priests and the high priest. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter gives rules for priestly mourning and marriage, adds stricter requirements for the high priest, and describes physical conditions that restrict altar service while preserving access to holy food.
chapters.studyObservation: Distinguish limits on particular sanctuary duties from exclusion from all priestly provision. The high priest's responsibilities differ from those of other priests and are explained in relation to sanctuary holiness.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 22 continues with priestly access to holy food. Hebrews 4–5 discusses Jesus as high priest in a distinct Christian theological framework.
studyQuestions: Which responsibilities are specific to the high priest?
What distinction is made between altar service and receiving holy food?
How can dignity be upheld while recognising the ancient ritual setting?
chapters.lifeApplication: Those entrusted with leadership should accept accountability and treat sacred responsibilities carefully; communities should preserve the dignity and provision of people whose circumstances limit particular roles.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Never use this chapter to demean people with disabilities or claim bodily difference makes someone morally inferior or rejected by God; the text concerns defined ritual duties.
chapters.readingNote: Compare the requirements for ordinary priests and the high priest, then note the provision concerning holy food and continue into chapter 22.

chapters.title: Leviticus 22 — Holy offerings and priestly access
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 22 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on priestly access to sacred food, acceptable offerings and the distinction between holy and ordinary. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter explains when priests may eat sacred food, who may receive priestly portions, and what makes an animal offering acceptable; it includes rules about defects, age and dedicated things.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the repeated concern that offerings be appropriate to their purpose. The chapter distinguishes ordinary food from holy portions and makes careful provision for the priest's household.
chapters.connectionNotes: Leviticus 7 explains priestly portions, and Deuteronomy 15:19–23 gives related firstborn-animal instructions; later Christian offering language belongs to a different covenant setting.
studyQuestions: When may a priest not eat holy food?
Who may eat the priestly portions?
What makes an animal acceptable or unacceptable as an offering?
chapters.lifeApplication: Handle resources entrusted to a community with integrity and transparency, without exploiting people under the language of religious giving.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The requirement for an unblemished sacrificial animal is not a judgement that people with disabilities are unacceptable to God; these rules concern offerings and ritual access.
chapters.readingNote: Read verses 1–16 separately from the animal rules in verses 17–33, noting the repeated concern that the Lord's name and holy things not be profaned.

chapters.title: Leviticus 23 — The appointed feasts of the Lord
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 23 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on Israel's calendar of weekly Sabbath, annual festivals, harvest and sacred assemblies. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter lists Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks, the trumpet observance, the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Booths, with dates and communal requirements.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the sequence and distinct themes of deliverance, harvest, repentance and wilderness remembrance. The harvest instructions include provision for poor people and resident foreigners.
chapters.connectionNotes: Exodus 12 gives Passover context, Deuteronomy 16 summarises pilgrimage festivals, and Acts 2 describes Pentecost in a later historical setting; Christian traditions differ in application.
studyQuestions: Which appointed times are listed and in what order?
How do festivals connect worship with harvest and remembrance?
Where does the chapter include provision for poor people and foreigners?
chapters.lifeApplication: Build rhythms of remembrance, gratitude, rest and generosity, and let celebration include people who might otherwise be left out.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not collapse all festivals into one generic celebration or assume every Christian tradition observes them identically; the calendar belongs to Israel's covenant and agricultural setting.
chapters.readingNote: Map the festivals in order, note dates and rest requirements, and pay attention to the provision for the poor and resident foreigner in the harvest instructions.

chapters.title: Leviticus 24 — The lamp, bread and justice in the camp
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 24 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on regular sanctuary service followed by a public legal case and principles of equal justice. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The priests maintain the lamp and arrange twelve loaves each Sabbath. A case involving blasphemy is brought to Moses, followed by rulings concerning injury, death and equal treatment.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the shift from regular sanctuary care to a public legal case. The twelve loaves are eaten by priests in a holy place, while the legal section applies the same standard to resident foreigner and native.
chapters.connectionNotes: Exodus 25 and 27 describe the lamp and table. Matthew 5 discusses responses to injury in a different teaching context, so do not assume every later teaching has the same legal function.
studyQuestions: What regular duties are assigned to priests?
How is the legal case brought before Moses and resolved?
What does the chapter say about equal standards of justice?
chapters.lifeApplication: Care for shared responsibilities and insist on impartial justice; apply standards consistently regardless of background or social standing.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not use the blasphemy narrative to justify persecution or mob violence. The ruling is a specific covenant judgement, not permission for private retaliation.
chapters.readingNote: Read the sanctuary instructions before the narrative and legal ruling, then consider the equality clause for resident foreigner and native in verses 22–23.

chapters.title: Leviticus 25 — Sabbath year and Jubilee
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 25 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on land rest, ancestral holdings, redemption, poverty and freedom under the conviction that the land belongs to God. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter regulates the seventh-year rest and the Jubilee after seven cycles of seven years, including return of ancestral holdings, redemption of property and support for impoverished Israelites.
chapters.studyObservation: Land is not treated as an unlimited commodity: values are related to harvest years because the land belongs to the Lord. The laws warn against exploiting a poor neighbour and support family redemption.
chapters.connectionNotes: Exodus 23 describes a sabbath year, Deuteronomy 15 addresses debt and care for the poor, and Luke 4 uses release language in Jesus' mission in a related but distinct setting.
studyQuestions: What happens to the land in the seventh year?
How does Jubilee affect ancestral property and family redemption?
What protections are given to an impoverished neighbour?
chapters.lifeApplication: Consider how economic arrangements can protect families from permanent dispossession and how communities can support people facing hardship.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not present Jubilee as a ready-made modern economic blueprint without considering its ancient land, kinship and covenant setting or inventing administrative details.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the seven-year pattern and Jubilee proclamation, then compare land redemption with lending and servitude; keep divine ownership central.

chapters.title: Leviticus 26 — Covenant blessings, warnings and restoration
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 26 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on promises, escalating covenant warnings, exile imagery, confession and God's remembrance. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter promises rain, harvest, peace and God's presence for covenant faithfulness, warns of escalating consequences for rejection, and closes with confession and remembrance of the covenant.
chapters.studyObservation: Observe the progression from blessing to increasingly severe warnings and then the possibility of confession and restoration. The land's sabbath rest is connected with exile, while covenant faithfulness remains central.
chapters.connectionNotes: Deuteronomy 28 contains a related but distinct blessing-and-curse section; Nehemiah 9 recalls Israel's disobedience and God's mercy in a later historical setting.
studyQuestions: What blessings are associated with covenant faithfulness?
How do the warnings intensify?
What hope remains when the people confess and humble themselves?
chapters.lifeApplication: Let gratitude, obedience and communal responsibility shape faithfulness; when failure occurs, pursue honest confession and repair rather than denial or despair.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not apply national covenant consequences directly to an individual's illness, poverty or hardship; this chapter is not a formula for blaming sufferers.
chapters.readingNote: Read the warnings as a structured sequence and do not skip the closing verses about confession and covenant remembrance; compare Deuteronomy 28 carefully.

chapters.title: Leviticus 27 — Vows, valuations and dedicated property
chapters.historicalContext: Leviticus 27 belongs to the book's unfolding account of Israel's covenant worship and communal life. This chapter focuses on vows concerning persons, animals, houses and land, redemption and the distinction of tithes. Its instructions must be read within the sanctuary, priesthood and covenant setting rather than detached from the book's historical and literary sequence.
chapters.overview: The chapter assigns valuations for persons dedicated by vow, allows adjustment for someone unable to pay, regulates animals and property, and distinguishes dedicated things from tithes and firstborn animals.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the distinction between a vow and an ordinary gift. Some things are devoted irrevocably, while other property may be redeemed with an added fifth; the closing verses identify the tithe as belonging to the Lord.
chapters.connectionNotes: Numbers 18 gives further instructions about tithes and priestly support. Deuteronomy 23 urges care in making vows, and Matthew 5 warns against manipulative oath-making in a distinct setting.
studyQuestions: How are valuations adjusted for someone unable to pay?
Which dedicated items may be redeemed and what is added?
How does the chapter distinguish vows from tithes and firstborn animals?
chapters.lifeApplication: Make commitments thoughtfully and keep promises with integrity; give freely and transparently without pressuring others or promising beyond what can responsibly be fulfilled.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not use the valuation schedule to price human worth or pressure people into giving; the chapter itself allows adjustment for someone unable to meet the stated valuation.
chapters.readingNote: Read the sections in sequence and distinguish vows concerning persons, animals, houses, fields and tithes; note that this appendix follows the covenant blessings and warnings.
